headline: Listening to Forests: Ecologist Wins $100K Award for Sound Science
meta_description: Tropical forest ecologist Zuzana Burivalova wins 2026 Pritzker Environmental Genius Award for using sound recordings to track forest health worldwide.
summary_short: A researcher who listens to forests with remote audio recorders has won a major environmental prize and $100,000 to expand her groundbreaking work.
body:
Zuzana Burivalova, an associate professor at the University of Wisconsin–Madison, has won the 2026 Pritzker Emerging Environmental Genius Award for pioneering a method that sounds deceptively simple but reveals profound truths: placing remote audio recorders deep in tropical forests to listen, continuously, to the pulse of life. By capturing the sounds of mammals, birds, amphibians, and insects across forests in Papua New Guinea, Indonesia, Peru, Madagascar, and Ecuador, Burivalova and her team have created acoustic baselines that show what healthy forest soundscapes sound like—and, critically, how they change over time. The $100,000 prize recognizes not just innovation but a quiet revolution in how we measure and understand biodiversity health.

Burivalova told Mongabay that receiving the award felt especially meaningful "during times that are challenging for work in environmental issues and conservation." She emphasized the responsibility it carries: "I see getting an award like this to also mean taking the responsibility for doing as much as I can for biodiversity conservation in the years to come." Her Sound Forest Lab's work has become so credible that it now collaborates with major conservation platforms examining which strategies actually work on the ground.

The researcher plans to use the prize money to scale the Soundscape Baselines Project, partnering with more local scientists and communities in intact forest areas—a deliberate choice to center indigenous knowledge alongside acoustic science. She also aims to build a portfolio showing exactly how soundscape baselines translate into real conservation action. Two other finalists, forest restoration pioneer Doris Njagi and microbial ecologist Suzanne Pierre, each received $15,000. Burivalova called them inspiring, recognizing that listening to forests is just one thread in a broader tapestry of conservation work being woven quietly, persistently, by people determined to protect what remains.
quick_facts: Zuzana Burivalova uses remote audio recorders to monitor forest health
Works across five tropical regions: Papua New Guinea, Indonesia, Peru, Madagascar, Ecuador
Won $100,000 to expand Soundscape Baselines Project with local partners
Award from UCLA's Institute of the Environment and Sustainability
